answers.question: Why was Java 8 introduced over Java 7, and what are its major features?
answers.shortTitle: Why Java 8 was introduced — lambdas, streams, Optional, java.time, default methods

s1_definition.profdef: Java 8 (2014) was the biggest Java release ever. It introduced: **Lambda expressions** (concise anonymous functions — pass behavior as data), **Functional interfaces** (SAM interfaces: `Predicate`, `Function`, `Consumer`, `Supplier`), **Stream API** (declarative data processing pipelines — filter/map/reduce), **Optional** (null-safe container — eliminates NullPointerException), **default/static methods in interfaces** (backward-compatible API evolution — `Collection.stream()` added without breaking implementations), **Method references** (`Trade::getAmount` instead of `t -> t.getAmount()`), **java.time API** (immutable, thread-safe dates — replaced broken `Date`/`Calendar`), **CompletableFuture** (async composition), **Parallel streams** (multi-core processing with one method call).
s1_definition.analogy: Before Java 8, processing 100,000 trades required 50 lines of for-loops, temporary lists, and manual threading. After Java 8: `trades.stream().filter(t -> t.isActive()).map(Trade::getAmount).reduce(BigDecimal.ZERO, BigDecimal::add)` — one readable pipeline that can parallelize with `.parallelStream()`. It changed Java from purely imperative to a hybrid OOP + functional language.
s1_definition.oneliner: Java 8 = lambdas + streams + Optional + java.time + default methods. Changed Java from imperative loops to declarative pipelines.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Java 8 (2014) was the biggest Java release ever. It introduced: **Lambda expressions** (concise anonymous functions — pass behavior as data), **Functional interfaces** (SAM interfaces: `Predicate`, `Function`, `Consumer`, `Supplier`), **Stream API** (declarative data processing pipelines — filter/map/reduce), **Optional** (null-safe container — eliminates NullPointerException), **default/static methods in interfaces** (backward-compatible API evolution — `Collection.stream()` added without breaking implementations), **Method references** (`Trade::getAmount` instead of `t -> t.getAmount()`), **java.time API** (immutable, thread-safe dates — replaced broken `Date`/`Calendar`), **CompletableFuture** (async composition), **Parallel streams** (multi-core processing with one method call).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Before Java 8, processing 100,000 trades required 50 lines of for-loops, temporary lists, and manual threading. After Java 8: `trades.stream().filter(t -> t.isActive()).map(Trade::getAmount).reduce(BigDecimal.ZERO, BigDecimal::add)` — one readable pipeline that can parallelize with `.parallelStream()`. It changed Java from purely imperative to a hybrid OOP + functional language.

**One line to remember:** Java 8 = lambdas + streams + Optional + java.time + default methods. Changed Java from imperative loops to declarative pipelines.

sections.s2_technical:
Java 8 added several pillars that work together. `Lambda expressions` let you pass behaviour as data instead of writing an anonymous class. For example, filtering active trades becomes `trades.stream().filter(t -> t.isActive())` instead of a verbose `new Predicate(){...}`.

`Functional interfaces` are the types lambdas target — single-abstract-method interfaces like `Predicate<T>`, `Function<T,R>`, `Consumer<T>`, and `Supplier<T>`. The `Stream API` provides declarative pipelines: `accounts.stream().map(Account::getBalance).reduce(BigDecimal.ZERO, BigDecimal::add)` sums balances without an explicit loop.

`Optional<T>` wraps a possibly-absent value so you handle null explicitly: `repo.findById("SAV2001").map(Account::getBalance).orElse(BigDecimal.ZERO)`. `Default methods` let interfaces evolve without breaking implementers — `Collection.stream()` was added as a default. The `java.time` API (`LocalDate`, `Instant`, `ZonedDateTime`) replaced the non-thread-safe `Date`/`Calendar`. Method references like `Trade::getAmount` make lambdas even terser. Senior nuance: streams are lazy — nothing runs until a terminal operation, which lets the pipeline fuse operations and short-circuit.
sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The bank's daily settlement report was written in Java 7 style:** 50 lines of for-loops, temporary ArrayLists, manual null checks, and SimpleDateFormat (not thread-safe). The team rewrites it using Java 8 features: Stream pipeline replaces loops, Optional replaces null checks, java.time replaces Date/Calendar, lambda replaces anonymous inner class.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a list of three trades for account SAV2001 with amounts Rs.50,000, Rs.150,000 and Rs.2,00,000; we want the total of trades above Rs.1,00,000.

Step 1. The source list enters `trades.stream()`. No data is processed yet — the pipeline is only described, not executed. The data still lives in the original list, unchanged.

Step 2. `.filter(t -> t.getAmount().compareTo(LIMIT) > 0)` is declared as an intermediate operation. It is lazy, so still nothing runs; the filter predicate is just remembered.

Step 3. `.map(Trade::getAmount)` is declared — it will transform each surviving Trade into its BigDecimal amount when the pipeline finally runs.

Step 4. `.reduce(BigDecimal.ZERO, BigDecimal::add)` is a terminal operation. Now the whole pipeline executes: the Rs.50,000 trade is dropped by the filter, the Rs.150,000 and Rs.2,00,000 trades pass, their amounts are extracted and added.

Step 5. The reduce produces Rs.3,50,000. The original list is still intact.

```text
INFO: Java8 pipeline total of large trades = 350000
```
sections.s5c_hld:
HLD is the rooftop view of the whole system. "Why Java 8" is the umbrella topic — lambdas, streams, Optional, java.time, and default methods together moved Java from purely imperative to a hybrid functional style. Architecturally these features let a banking platform be written as declarative pipelines (stream filter/map/reduce), pass behaviour as data (lambdas into services), avoid NullPointerException at API boundaries (Optional return types), handle time correctly (java.time), and evolve shared interfaces without breaking callers (default methods). The HLD shows a modern Java 8 banking service that uses all five.

For this topic, National Bank of India's account service demonstrates the Java 8 toolkit end to end: a stream pipeline summarises accounts, a lambda injects a rule, Optional guards a lookup, java.time stamps the record, and a default method on a shared interface adds behaviour for free.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Java 8 was the most significant release in Java's history, transforming the language from purely imperative to a hybrid object-oriented and functional style. Lambda expressions pass behavior as data, eliminating verbose anonymous inner classes. The Stream API provides declarative data processing pipelines: filter, map, reduce, collect replace manual for-loops with readable, composable operations. Optional eliminates NullPointerException by forcing explicit handling of absent values. The java.time API replaced the broken, mutable, non-thread-safe Date and Calendar classes with immutable, thread-safe LocalDate, LocalDateTime, and ZonedDateTime. Default methods on interfaces enabled backward-compatible API evolution, allowing Collection.stream() to be added without breaking existing implementations.

In my settlement report service, the Java 7 version required 50 lines of imperative code with manual counters, null checks, and anonymous Comparator classes. The Java 8 version produces the identical report in 15 lines of declarative stream pipelines. The stream approach is also easier to parallelize: replacing stream() with parallelStream() distributes the work across multiple cores with zero code changes. Method references like Trade::getAmount and Trade::isSettled make the code read like English. The combination of streams, lambdas, Optional, and java.time is now the standard way to write Java in every modern banking application.

answers.question: What is the Java 8 java.time Date/Time API, and why is it preferred over legacy Date/Calendar/SimpleDateFormat? What is Instant vs ZonedDateTime?
answers.shortTitle: java.time Date/Time API — LocalDate, ZonedDateTime, Instant, Duration, vs legacy Date/Calendar

s1_definition.profdef: `java.time` (JSR-310): immutable, thread-safe date/time classes. `LocalDate` = date without time (2024-01-15). `LocalTime` = time without date (14:30:00). `LocalDateTime` = date + time without timezone. `ZonedDateTime` = date + time + timezone (for display to humans). `Instant` = UTC machine timestamp (for storage/comparison). `Duration` = time-based amount (5 seconds, 2 hours). `Period` = date-based amount (3 months, 1 year). `DateTimeFormatter` = thread-safe formatting (unlike `SimpleDateFormat`). Legacy `Date`/`Calendar` problems: mutable (thread-unsafe), months 0-based (January=0), `SimpleDateFormat` not thread-safe, no separation of date/time/zone.
s1_definition.analogy: `Instant` = the vault's atomic clock timestamp (UTC, machine-precise, stored in DB). `ZonedDateTime` = what the Mumbai branch teller sees on their wall clock (IST = UTC+5:30). `LocalDate` = the date stamped on a cheque (no time, no zone). `Duration` = "this transaction took 250 milliseconds." `Period` = "your FD tenure is 1 year 6 months."
s1_definition.oneliner: Instant = UTC machine timestamp (store in DB). ZonedDateTime = human display with timezone. LocalDate = date only. All immutable + thread-safe. Never use Date/Calendar/SimpleDateFormat.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `java.time` (JSR-310): immutable, thread-safe date/time classes. `LocalDate` = date without time (2024-01-15). `LocalTime` = time without date (14:30:00). `LocalDateTime` = date + time without timezone. `ZonedDateTime` = date + time + timezone (for display to humans). `Instant` = UTC machine timestamp (for storage/comparison). `Duration` = time-based amount (5 seconds, 2 hours). `Period` = date-based amount (3 months, 1 year). `DateTimeFormatter` = thread-safe formatting (unlike `SimpleDateFormat`). Legacy `Date`/`Calendar` problems: mutable (thread-unsafe), months 0-based (January=0), `SimpleDateFormat` not thread-safe, no separation of date/time/zone.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** `Instant` = the vault's atomic clock timestamp (UTC, machine-precise, stored in DB). `ZonedDateTime` = what the Mumbai branch teller sees on their wall clock (IST = UTC+5:30). `LocalDate` = the date stamped on a cheque (no time, no zone). `Duration` = "this transaction took 250 milliseconds." `Period` = "your FD tenure is 1 year 6 months."

**One line to remember:** Instant = UTC machine timestamp (store in DB). ZonedDateTime = human display with timezone. LocalDate = date only. All immutable + thread-safe. Never use Date/Calendar/SimpleDateFormat.

sections.s2_technical:
The `java.time` API is immutable and thread-safe, unlike the old `Date`/`Calendar`. `LocalDate` is a date with no time or zone — `LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 31)` models a financial year-end. `LocalDateTime` adds a time but still no zone. `Instant` is a point on the UTC timeline, ideal for timestamps: `Instant.now()`.

`ZonedDateTime` ties an instant to a zone — essential when a Mumbai settlement at `ZoneId.of("Asia/Kolkata")` must be shown to a London desk. `Duration` measures machine time (seconds/nanos) between two Instants: `Duration.between(start, end).toMillis()` times a settlement run. `Period` measures human time (years/months/days): `Period.between(openDate, LocalDate.now()).getYears()` gives an account's age.

Because every object is immutable, methods return new copies: `maturity = deposit.plusMonths(6)` leaves `deposit` unchanged, so two threads computing interest never corrupt each other. Senior nuance: store timestamps as `Instant` (UTC) and convert to a zone only for display; never store wall-clock times without a zone.
sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The bank's FD maturity calculator uses legacy `Date` and `SimpleDateFormat`.** Two threads formatting dates simultaneously corrupt the output (SimpleDateFormat is not thread-safe). Month off-by-one bugs: `new Date(2024, 0, 15)` — January is 0! The team migrates to `java.time`: immutable, thread-safe, readable month names, proper timezone handling for international customers.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a fixed deposit opened on `2026-01-31` with a 6-month term; we compute the maturity date and how many days remain from `2026-03-01`.

Step 1. `LocalDate open = LocalDate.of(2026,1,31)` creates an immutable date object held on the heap.

Step 2. `LocalDate maturity = open.plusMonths(6)` does NOT change `open`; it returns a brand new `LocalDate` of `2026-07-31`. The original `open` still reads `2026-01-31`.

Step 3. `LocalDate today = LocalDate.of(2026,3,1)` is created as the reference point.

Step 4. `Period p = Period.between(today, maturity)` computes human-readable distance; `long days = ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(today, maturity)` computes exact days (152).

Step 5. The result objects are returned; every input date remains unchanged because the API is immutable.

```text
INFO: maturity=2026-07-31 daysRemaining=152
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ java.time CLASS HIERARCHY ═══

  LocalDate       → date only: 2024-01-15 (cheque date, FD maturity date)
  LocalTime       → time only: 14:30:00 (market open time)
  LocalDateTime   → date + time: 2024-01-15T14:30:00 (trade execution time, no zone)
  ZonedDateTime   → date + time + zone: 2024-01-15T14:30:00+05:30[Asia/Kolkata] (customer display)
  Instant         → UTC timestamp: 2024-01-15T09:00:00Z (DB storage, comparison, ordering)

  Duration        → time-based: PT5S (5 seconds), PT2H (2 hours) — for measuring elapsed time
  Period          → date-based: P1Y6M (1 year 6 months) — for FD tenure, loan tenure

  DateTimeFormatter → THREAD-SAFE formatting (static final OK — share across threads)

  ═══ Instant vs ZonedDateTime ═══

  Instant now = Instant.now();  // UTC: 2024-01-15T09:00:00Z

  Mumbai:  now.atZone(ZoneId.of("Asia/Kolkata"))  → 2024-01-15T14:30:00+05:30
  London:  now.atZone(ZoneId.of("Europe/London")) → 2024-01-15T09:00:00+00:00
  NewYork: now.atZone(ZoneId.of("America/New_York")) → 2024-01-15T04:00:00-05:00

  SAME INSTANT, DIFFERENT DISPLAY. Store Instant in DB. Convert to ZonedDateTime for UI.

  ═══ Legacy vs java.time ═══

  Legacy Date:           Mutable! date.setMonth(5) changes the object.
  java.time LocalDate:   IMMUTABLE! date.plusMonths(5) returns NEW object.

  Legacy Calendar:       Months 0-based! Calendar.JANUARY = 0.
  java.time:             Months 1-based! Month.JANUARY = 1.

  Legacy SimpleDateFormat: NOT thread-safe! Shared instance → corrupt output.
  java.time DateTimeFormatter: THREAD-SAFE! Static final shared safely.

  ═══ DB STORAGE RULE ═══

  Store: Instant → TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE (always UTC in DB)
  Display: convert to ZonedDateTime with customer's timezone
  Never store LocalDateTime in DB (no timezone info → ambiguous!)
```
sections.s5c_hld:
HLD is the rooftop view of the whole system. The architectural driver for java.time is correctness across time zones and immutability for thread safety. In a banking platform that spans customers, exchanges, and settlement cycles, you must store an unambiguous instant (Instant/UTC) in the database, convert to the customer's zone (ZonedDateTime) only at the edges, and compute durations (Duration/Period) for interest and maturity. Because every java.time type is immutable, these values are safe to share across threads without locks. The HLD shows the Scheduling/Interest Service relying on java.time for every date computation.

For this topic, National Bank of India computes a fixed deposit's maturity date and accrued interest. The service stores the open time as a UTC Instant, displays it to Rajesh in Asia/Kolkata via ZonedDateTime, and uses LocalDate.plusMonths for maturity — all immutable, all thread-safe.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The java.time API introduced in Java 8 replaced the broken Date, Calendar, and SimpleDateFormat classes. All java.time classes are immutable and thread-safe: calling plusMonths on a LocalDate returns a new object, the original is unchanged. This eliminates an entire category of concurrency bugs that plagued legacy Date code. Months are 1-based (January equals 1), fixing the confusing 0-based months in Calendar.

The key distinction is between Instant and ZonedDateTime. Instant is a UTC machine timestamp — store it in the database as TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE. ZonedDateTime is the same instant displayed in a specific timezone — use it for customer-facing output. The same Instant shows as 2:30 PM in Mumbai and 9:00 AM in London. DateTimeFormatter is thread-safe and can be a static final field shared across all threads, unlike SimpleDateFormat which corrupts output when shared. In my FD maturity calculator, LocalDate handles deposit and maturity dates, Period calculates "1 year 6 months" tenure, Duration measures processing time, and Instant plus ZonedDateTime handle UTC storage with timezone-aware display for international customers.

answers.question: What is the Java 8 Base64 API (getEncoder/getDecoder, URL-safe, MIME variants), when do you use Base64, and why is it encoding NOT encryption?
answers.shortTitle: Java 8 Base64 API — encoding/decoding, URL-safe, MIME, encoding vs encryption

s1_definition.profdef: `Base64` converts binary data into ASCII text using 64 printable characters (A-Z, a-z, 0-9, +, /). Three variants: **Basic** (standard — for general encoding), **URL-safe** (replaces `+/` with `-_` — safe in URLs/query params), **MIME** (line-wrapped at 76 chars — for email attachments). Use cases: encode binary in JSON (`byte[]` → string), JWT payload (header.payload.signature are Base64URL-encoded), file content in REST APIs, basic auth headers. **Base64 is encoding, NOT encryption:** anyone can decode it. It provides NO security — it just makes binary transportable as text. For security: use AES encryption, then optionally Base64-encode the ciphertext for transport.
s1_definition.analogy: Base64 is like writing a cheque amount in words ("Five Thousand Rupees Only") instead of numbers. Anyone can read it — it is NOT a secret code. It is just a different REPRESENTATION of the same data. Encryption would be putting the cheque in a locked vault (AES) — only the key holder can read it.
s1_definition.oneliner: Base64 = binary to text (encoding, NOT encryption). Basic for general. URL-safe for URLs/JWT. MIME for email. Anyone can decode — zero security.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `Base64` converts binary data into ASCII text using 64 printable characters (A-Z, a-z, 0-9, +, /). Three variants: **Basic** (standard — for general encoding), **URL-safe** (replaces `+/` with `-_` — safe in URLs/query params), **MIME** (line-wrapped at 76 chars — for email attachments). Use cases: encode binary in JSON (`byte[]` → string), JWT payload (header.payload.signature are Base64URL-encoded), file content in REST APIs, basic auth headers. **Base64 is encoding, NOT encryption:** anyone can decode it. It provides NO security — it just makes binary transportable as text. For security: use AES encryption, then optionally Base64-encode the ciphertext for transport.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Base64 is like writing a cheque amount in words ("Five Thousand Rupees Only") instead of numbers. Anyone can read it — it is NOT a secret code. It is just a different REPRESENTATION of the same data. Encryption would be putting the cheque in a locked vault (AES) — only the key holder can read it.

**One line to remember:** Base64 = binary to text (encoding, NOT encryption). Basic for general. URL-safe for URLs/JWT. MIME for email. Anyone can decode — zero security.

sections.s2_technical:
Java 8's `java.util.Base64` turns raw bytes into safe ASCII text and back. It is encoding, NOT encryption — anyone can decode it, so it never protects secrets; it only makes binary data transport-safe (for example, embedding a digital signature inside a JSON payment message).

`Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(bytes)` produces standard Base64. `Base64.getDecoder().decode(str)` reverses it. For data placed in a URL or filename, `Base64.getUrlEncoder()` replaces `+` and `/` with `-` and `_` so the string survives URL parsing: `Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding().encodeToString(token)`.

For long payloads like an encoded statement PDF, `Base64.getMimeEncoder()` inserts line breaks every 76 characters per the MIME standard. A typical banking use: encode an HMAC signature of a transfer request so it can travel as a header. Senior nuance: Base64 inflates size by about 33%, so do not Base64 large blobs in hot paths; and because it is reversible, always pair it with real cryptography (HMAC/AES) when integrity or confidentiality matters.
sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The bank's document service stores customer KYC documents (Aadhaar scan, PAN card image) as Base64-encoded strings in JSON API responses.** The mobile app sends documents as Base64 in the request body. JWT tokens use Base64URL encoding for the header and payload. The team needs to understand: when to use which variant, why Base64 is NOT encryption (a common misconception), and how to properly secure sensitive documents (AES encrypt THEN Base64 encode).

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a transfer reference string `"SAV2001:CUR3001:50000"` that must travel safely inside a URL query parameter.

Step 1. The string is converted to bytes with `ref.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)`. The data is now a raw byte array in memory.

Step 2. `Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding().encodeToString(bytes)` transforms those bytes into URL-safe ASCII, e.g. `U0FWMjAwMTpDVVIzMDAxOjUwMDAw`. The original bytes are untouched; a new String is produced.

Step 3. The encoded token is placed in the URL and sent. No `+`, `/`, or `=` characters appear, so the URL parser does not mangle it.

Step 4. The receiver calls `Base64.getUrlDecoder().decode(token)` to get the original byte array back.

Step 5. `new String(bytes, UTF_8)` reconstructs `"SAV2001:CUR3001:50000"` exactly. The round trip is lossless because Base64 is a reversible mapping.

```text
INFO: encoded=U0FWMjAwMTpDVVIzMDAxOjUwMDAw decoded=SAV2001:CUR3001:50000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ THREE BASE64 VARIANTS ═══

  BASIC:    A-Z, a-z, 0-9, +, /    Padding: =
    Use: JSON body, DB storage, general binary-to-text
    Example: SGVsbG8gV29ybGQ=

  URL-SAFE: A-Z, a-z, 0-9, -, _    No padding (optional)
    Use: JWT tokens, URL query params, file download links
    Example: SGVsbG8gV29ybGQ
    + replaced with -   (+ means space in URLs)
    / replaced with _   (/ is path separator in URLs)
    = removed           (= is assignment in query params)

  MIME:     Same as Basic + line breaks every 76 chars
    Use: Email attachments (SMTP line length limit)
    Rarely used in REST APIs.

  ═══ BASE64 IN JWT ═══

  JWT: eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJyYWplc2gifQ.signature
       ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ^^^^^^^^^
       header (Base64URL)        payload (Base64URL)      HMAC signature

  Header + Payload: ANYONE can decode → they are PUBLIC, not secret!
  Signature: created with SECRET KEY → provides INTEGRITY (tamper detection)
  NEVER put sensitive data in JWT payload (account balances, passwords)!

  ═══ ENCODING vs ENCRYPTION ═══

  Base64 ENCODING: binary → text. ANYONE can reverse. Zero security.
    "Hello" → "SGVsbG8=" → "Hello"

  AES ENCRYPTION: plaintext + KEY → ciphertext. Only KEY holder can reverse.
    "Hello" + key → 0xA3F2... → "Hello" (only with correct key!)

  CORRECT for sensitive data:
    Step 1: AES encrypt (security)
    Step 2: Base64 encode the ciphertext (transport as text)
    Receiver: Base64 decode → AES decrypt with key
```
sections.s5c_hld:
HLD is the rooftop view of the whole system. The architectural truth about Base64 is that it is a TRANSPORT ENCODING, not security: it turns binary (a KYC PDF, a card image) into text that safely travels inside JSON bodies, URLs, and JWT tokens. In a banking platform the HLD must show WHERE encoding happens and, crucially, where real security (TLS in transit, AES at rest) is layered on top — because Base64 alone protects nothing. The Document Service encodes files for the API response; the Security layer handles actual confidentiality.

For this topic, National Bank of India's document service returns Rajesh's KYC document inside a JSON API response. The binary PDF is Base64-encoded so it survives JSON transport; for sensitive fields the ciphertext is AES-encrypted first, THEN Base64-encoded.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Java 8 Base64 API provides three variants: Basic encoder for general binary-to-text conversion used in JSON bodies and database storage, URL-safe encoder that replaces plus and slash with hyphen and underscore for use in URLs, query parameters, and JWT tokens, and MIME encoder that wraps lines at 76 characters for email attachments. Base64 increases data size by approximately 33 percent because it represents 3 bytes of binary as 4 ASCII characters.

The critical distinction is that Base64 is encoding, NOT encryption. Anyone can decode a Base64 string without any key. It provides zero security — it merely converts binary data into a text-safe format for transport. In my banking document service, KYC documents are Base64-encoded for transmission in JSON API responses, but they are NOT secured by this encoding. For sensitive data like account numbers or card details, the correct approach is AES encryption first, then Base64 encoding of the ciphertext for transport. JWT tokens use Base64URL encoding for the header and payload, which means anyone can decode and read them — sensitive data should never be stored in JWT payloads. Only the signature provides integrity through HMAC with a secret key.

### 6.2 Lambda expressions (Q4 of 125)

answers.question: What is a lambda expression, and what are its advantages over anonymous classes?
answers.shortTitle: Lambda expressions — what they are, advantages over anonymous classes

s1_definition.profdef: A lambda is a concise anonymous function: `(parameters) -> expression/body`. It implements a functional interface's single abstract method (SAM) without the boilerplate of an anonymous class. Advantages: less code (1 line vs 5+), no `.class` file generated, enables functional programming (pass behavior as data), type inference (compiler infers parameter types), enables method references (`Trade::getAmount`), captures effectively-final variables.
s1_definition.oneliner: Lambda = concise anonymous function. `(params) -> body`. Replaces anonymous class. Enables functional programming.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A lambda is a concise anonymous function: `(parameters) -> expression/body`. It implements a functional interface's single abstract method (SAM) without the boilerplate of an anonymous class. Advantages: less code (1 line vs 5+), no `.class` file generated, enables functional programming (pass behavior as data), type inference (compiler infers parameter types), enables method references (`Trade::getAmount`), captures effectively-final variables.

**One line to remember:** Lambda = concise anonymous function. `(params) -> body`. Replaces anonymous class. Enables functional programming.

sections.s2_technical:
A lambda expression is a concise way to implement a functional interface's single abstract method. The syntax is `(parameters) -> body`. For example, a `Predicate<Trade>` that keeps large trades is written `trade -> trade.getAmount().compareTo(LIMIT) > 0` instead of a five-line anonymous class.

Compared to an anonymous class, a lambda generates no extra synthetic `.class` file — the compiler emits an `invokedynamic` bootstrap, which keeps the artifact small. Also, inside a lambda `this` refers to the ENCLOSING instance, whereas in an anonymous class `this` refers to the anonymous object itself.

Lambdas enable passing behaviour as data: a `TradeFilterService.filter(List, Predicate)` method takes the rule as a parameter, so swapping "large trades" for "foreign trades" means passing a different lambda, not writing a new class. Lambdas can capture effectively-final local variables, which is how a runtime threshold is baked into the rule: `BigDecimal limit = new BigDecimal("100000"); Predicate<Trade> p = t -> t.amount().compareTo(limit) > 0;`. Senior nuance: prefer method references (`Trade::isActive`) when the lambda just forwards to an existing method.
sections.s3_banking: Problem — National Bank of India's trade filter needed many rules (large trades, foreign trades, suspicious trades) and the Java 7 code duplicated a five-line anonymous `Predicate` for each. Fix: lambdas let the filtering rule be passed as a one-line parameter, so a single `filter` method serves every criterion.

A lambda is a concise way to implement a functional interface's single method. It replaces the verbose anonymous inner class syntax with a single expression. answers.question: What is a lambda expression, and what are its advantages over anonymous classes?
answers.shortTitle: Lambda expressions — concise anonymous functions, advantages over anonymous classes

s1_definition.profdef: A lambda expression is a concise way to represent an anonymous function — a block of code that can be passed as an argument, stored in a variable, or returned from a method. Syntax: `(parameters) -> expression` or `(parameters) -> { statements; }`. It implements the single abstract method of a functional interface without the verbose boilerplate of an anonymous inner class. Advantages: 3-5x less code, no separate `.class` file generated at compile time (uses `invokedynamic` bytecode), enables functional programming style (pass behavior as data), type inference (compiler infers parameter types from context), enables method references (`Trade::getAmount`), and captures effectively-final local variables.
s1_definition.analogy: Before Java 8, to tell the bank's sorting system "sort trades by amount descending," you had to write a full Comparator class with 5 lines of boilerplate. With lambdas: `trades.sort((a, b) -> b.getAmount().compareTo(a.getAmount()))` — one line. It is like writing a quick instruction note instead of a formal 3-page memo for the same task.
s1_definition.oneliner: Lambda = `(params) -> body`. Replaces anonymous class. Enables passing behavior as data. Type-inferred. Captured variables must be effectively final.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A lambda expression is a concise way to represent an anonymous function — a block of code that can be passed as an argument, stored in a variable, or returned from a method. Syntax: `(parameters) -> expression` or `(parameters) -> { statements; }`. It implements the single abstract method of a functional interface without the verbose boilerplate of an anonymous inner class. Advantages: 3-5x less code, no separate `.class` file generated at compile time (uses `invokedynamic` bytecode), enables functional programming style (pass behavior as data), type inference (compiler infers parameter types from context), enables method references (`Trade::getAmount`), and captures effectively-final local variables.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Before Java 8, to tell the bank's sorting system "sort trades by amount descending," you had to write a full Comparator class with 5 lines of boilerplate. With lambdas: `trades.sort((a, b) -> b.getAmount().compareTo(a.getAmount()))` — one line. It is like writing a quick instruction note instead of a formal 3-page memo for the same task.

**One line to remember:** Lambda = `(params) -> body`. Replaces anonymous class. Enables passing behavior as data. Type-inferred. Captured variables must be effectively final.

sections.s2_technical:
**Lambda syntax.** Three forms:

`(Trade t) -> t.getAmount()` — explicit parameter type.

`t -> t.getAmount()` — inferred type (compiler knows from context).

`(t1, t2) -> { BigDecimal diff = t1.getAmount().subtract(t2.getAmount()); return diff.signum(); }` — multi-statement block with explicit return.

**Lambda vs anonymous class.** Lambda: no `new` keyword, no class name, no `@Override`, no curly braces for single expression. Anonymous: creates a separate inner `.class` file, has its own `this` reference (refers to the anonymous class), can implement interfaces with multiple abstract methods. Lambda `this` refers to the enclosing class (not the lambda itself).

**Effectively final capture.** A lambda can capture local variables from the enclosing scope, but they must be effectively final (not reassigned after initialization). This is because the lambda captures the VALUE (a copy), not the variable binding. If the variable changed after capture, the lambda would have a stale copy.

```java
BigDecimal threshold = new BigDecimal("100000"); // effectively final — never reassigned
Predicate<Trade> isLarge = t -> t.getAmount().compareTo(threshold) > 0;
// threshold = BigDecimal.ZERO; // COMPILE ERROR! Would make threshold NOT effectively final

// Workaround for mutable capture:
AtomicInteger counter = new AtomicInteger(0); // AtomicInteger is final, but its VALUE is mutable
trades.forEach(t -> counter.incrementAndGet()); // OK — counter reference is final
```

**invokedynamic.** Lambdas do NOT create anonymous classes at compile time. They use `invokedynamic` bytecode instruction which defers the implementation strategy to runtime. The JVM creates a lightweight implementation (often a method handle) without the overhead of a full class. This makes lambdas faster than anonymous classes for instantiation.
sections.s3_banking:

The team refactors to lambdas and method references: each Comparator becomes a one-liner, and common ones are shared as static constants.

**What the project will show:** Side-by-side anonymous class vs lambda for sorting, filtering, and processing trades. Demonstrates: single-expression lambda, multi-statement lambda, method reference, effectively-final capture, lambda composition (Comparator.comparing().thenComparing()), and the performance advantage (no .class file generation).

sections.s6_takeaway:
A lambda expression is a concise anonymous function that implements a functional interface's single abstract method. The syntax is parameters, arrow, and body: `(Trade t) -> t.getAmount()` for a single expression, or `(t1, t2) -> { return t1.compareTo(t2); }` for a multi-statement block. The compiler infers parameter types from the target context, so you can usually omit them: `t -> t.getAmount()`. Lambdas replace the verbose anonymous inner class pattern that required a class declaration, method override annotation, and curly braces for even the simplest operations.

In my trade sorting service, the anonymous class approach required 20 lines to sort, filter, and map trades: a 5-line Comparator anonymous class, a manual for-loop with an if-check for filtering, and another for-loop for mapping to DTOs. The lambda approach does the same in 4 lines: a stream pipeline with sorted using Comparator.comparing with a method reference, filter with a lambda predicate, and map with a lambda function. The lambda versions are not only shorter but composable: Comparator.comparing(Trade::getSymbol).thenComparing(Trade::getAmount, reverseOrder()) creates a multi-key sort in one expression.

Lambdas capture local variables from the enclosing scope, but those variables must be effectively final — never reassigned after initialization. This is because the lambda captures the value (a copy), not the variable binding. If the variable could change, the lambda would have a stale copy. The workaround for mutable capture is using AtomicInteger or a final array wrapper. Under the hood, lambdas use the invokedynamic bytecode instruction instead of generating anonymous class files, making them faster to instantiate and more memory-efficient. The `this` reference inside a lambda refers to the enclosing class, not the lambda itself — unlike anonymous classes where `this` refers to the anonymous class instance.

answers.question: What is target typing in lambda expressions, and why can a lambda be ambiguous with overloaded methods?
answers.shortTitle: Target typing and lambda ambiguity — compiler infers type from context

s1_definition.profdef: A lambda has no intrinsic type. The compiler infers the functional-interface type from the TARGET context: variable type, method parameter, return type, or cast. The SAME lambda `() -> "x"` can be `Supplier<String>` or `Callable<String>` depending on context. Ambiguity: if a method is overloaded accepting two different functional interfaces, the compiler cannot decide → compile error. Fix: explicit cast `method((Supplier<String>) () -> "x")`.
s1_definition.oneliner: A lambda has no type of its own — the compiler infers it from the target context, and when two overloads both match, you disambiguate with an explicit cast.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A lambda has no intrinsic type. The compiler infers the functional-interface type from the TARGET context: variable type, method parameter, return type, or cast. The SAME lambda `() -> "x"` can be `Supplier<String>` or `Callable<String>` depending on context. Ambiguity: if a method is overloaded accepting two different functional interfaces, the compiler cannot decide → compile error. Fix: explicit cast `method((Supplier<String>) () -> "x")`.

**One line to remember:** A lambda has no type of its own — the compiler infers it from the target context, and when two overloads both match, you disambiguate with an explicit cast.

sections.s2_technical:
Target typing means a lambda has no type of its own; the compiler infers it from the CONTEXT where the lambda appears — the "target type". The same lambda `x -> x` can be a `Function<Trade,Trade>` in one place and a `UnaryOperator<Trade>` in another, depending on the variable or parameter it is assigned to.

The target type can come from: an assignment (`Predicate<Trade> p = t -> t.isActive();`), a method parameter (`stream.filter(t -> t.isActive())`), a return statement, a cast (`(Comparator<Trade>) (a,b) -> ...`), or a ternary branch. The compiler checks that the lambda's parameter count and body type match the functional interface's single method.

Ambiguity arises with overloaded methods. If `settle(Predicate<Trade>)` and `settle(Function<Trade,Boolean>)` both exist, the call `settle(t -> t.isLarge())` is ambiguous because the lambda matches both shapes. The fix is to disambiguate with an explicit cast: `settle((Predicate<Trade>) t -> t.isLarge())`, or to avoid overloading functional parameters. Senior nuance: this is why library authors avoid overloads that differ only by functional-interface parameter type.
sections.s3_banking: Problem — A settlement API offered two overloaded `process` methods, one taking a `Predicate<Trade>` and one taking a `Function<Trade,Boolean>`; passing a bare lambda failed to compile with an ambiguity error. Fix: target typing is resolved by an explicit cast so the compiler knows which functional interface the lambda implements.

sections.s5c_hld:
HLD is the rooftop view of the whole system. The target-typing concept is about the compiler, not runtime wiring, but it still shapes API design across a banking platform: a lambda has no type of its own, so the compiler infers it from the target context (the variable type, method parameter, or return type it is assigned to). The same () -> "settled" can be a Supplier or a Callable depending on where it lands. Architecturally this means API designers must avoid overloading methods with different functional-interface parameters, otherwise callers hit ambiguity and need explicit casts. The HLD shows the shared API layer where these functional parameters are consumed.

answers.shortTitle: Target typing in lambdas — compiler infers type from context, overload ambiguity

s1_definition.profdef: A lambda has NO intrinsic type — it is not inherently a `Predicate` or `Function` or `Callable`. The compiler determines its type from the TARGET CONTEXT: the variable it is assigned to, the method parameter it is passed to, the return type expected, or an explicit cast. The SAME lambda `() -> "RELIANCE"` can be inferred as `Supplier<String>`, `Callable<String>`, or any functional interface with signature `() -> String`. Ambiguity occurs when an overloaded method accepts two different functional interfaces with compatible signatures — the compiler cannot choose and reports "reference to method is ambiguous." Fix: explicit cast `method((Supplier<String>) () -> "RELIANCE")`.
s1_definition.analogy: A lambda is like a blank cheque with the amount filled in but the payee line empty. The payee (type) is determined by WHERE you present the cheque: at the savings counter (Supplier), at the loan counter (Callable), at the insurance counter (Function). The SAME cheque works at any counter. But if two counters are side by side with identical forms (overloaded methods), the teller does not know which counter you want — you must point explicitly (cast).
s1_definition.oneliner: Lambda has no type. Compiler infers from context (variable, parameter, return, cast). Same lambda = different types. Overloaded methods with same-signature FIs = ambiguous → fix with cast.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A lambda has NO intrinsic type — it is not inherently a `Predicate` or `Function` or `Callable`. The compiler determines its type from the TARGET CONTEXT: the variable it is assigned to, the method parameter it is passed to, the return type expected, or an explicit cast. The SAME lambda `() -> "RELIANCE"` can be inferred as `Supplier<String>`, `Callable<String>`, or any functional interface with signature `() -> String`. Ambiguity occurs when an overloaded method accepts two different functional interfaces with compatible signatures — the compiler cannot choose and reports "reference to method is ambiguous." Fix: explicit cast `method((Supplier<String>) () -> "RELIANCE")`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A lambda is like a blank cheque with the amount filled in but the payee line empty. The payee (type) is determined by WHERE you present the cheque: at the savings counter (Supplier), at the loan counter (Callable), at the insurance counter (Function). The SAME cheque works at any counter. But if two counters are side by side with identical forms (overloaded methods), the teller does not know which counter you want — you must point explicitly (cast).

**One line to remember:** Lambda has no type. Compiler infers from context (variable, parameter, return, cast). Same lambda = different types. Overloaded methods with same-signature FIs = ambiguous → fix with cast.

sections.s3_banking:
**Problem — The bank's trade execution engine has two overloaded `execute` methods:** one accepts `Supplier<TradeResult>` for synchronous execution, another accepts `Callable<TradeResult>` for async execution with exception handling. When a developer passes a lambda `() -> executeTrade(order)`, the compiler reports "reference to execute is ambiguous" because both overloads match the lambda signature. The team needs to understand target typing and resolve the ambiguity with explicit casts.

**What the project will show:** Lambda type inference from 4 contexts (variable, parameter, return, cast), the overload ambiguity with side-by-side Supplier vs Callable, the fix with explicit cast, and why the compiler cannot decide.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Lambda `() -> new TradeResult(...)` has NO type. It is just a code block waiting to be typed.

**Step 2 — Variable context.** `Supplier<TradeResult> sync = () -> ...` — compiler sees the target variable is Supplier, so the lambda becomes Supplier. `Callable<TradeResult> async = () -> ...` — SAME lambda body, but target is Callable, so it becomes Callable.

**Step 3 — Method parameter context.** `executeSync(() -> ...)` — compiler sees executeSync accepts `Supplier<TradeResult>`, so lambda becomes Supplier. `executeAsync(() -> ...)` — compiler sees executeAsync accepts `Callable<TradeResult>`, so lambda becomes Callable.

**Step 4 — Return type context.** Method signature says `Supplier<TradeResult> createSupplier()`. The `return () -> ...` inside MUST be Supplier because that is the return type.

**Step 5 — Ambiguity.** `process(() -> ...)` where process is overloaded with Supplier AND Callable. Both match `() -> TradeResult`. Compiler cannot choose. COMPILE ERROR.

**Step 6 — Fix.** `process((Supplier<TradeResult>) () -> ...)` — the cast tells the compiler "this is a Supplier." Now unambiguous.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ TARGET TYPING — 4 CONTEXTS ═══

  Lambda: () -> new TradeResult("EXE", "RELIANCE", "FILLED", "?")
    │
    ├─ Context 1: Supplier<TradeResult> s = lambda;   → lambda IS Supplier
    ├─ Context 2: Callable<TradeResult> c = lambda;   → SAME lambda IS Callable
    ├─ Context 3: executeSync(lambda);                 → param type = Supplier → IS Supplier
    ├─ Context 4: return lambda; (method returns Supplier) → IS Supplier
    └─ Context 5: (Supplier<TradeResult>) lambda       → cast forces Supplier

  ═══ OVERLOAD AMBIGUITY ═══

  void process(Supplier<TradeResult> s) { }     // overload 1
  void process(Callable<TradeResult> c) { }     // overload 2

  process(() -> new TradeResult(...));           // COMPILE ERROR!
    │
    ├─ Supplier<T>.get():   () → T (no throws)    → lambda matches ✅
    ├─ Callable<T>.call():  () → T (throws Exception) → lambda matches ✅
    └─ TWO matches, ZERO preference → AMBIGUOUS!

  FIX:
    process((Supplier<TradeResult>) () -> ...);  → cast to Supplier ✅
    process((Callable<TradeResult>) () -> ...);  → cast to Callable ✅

  ═══ BEST PRACTICE ═══
  Avoid overloading methods with different functional interfaces that have
  the same lambda signature. Use different method NAMES instead:
    processSync(Supplier<T> s)   → unambiguous
    processAsync(Callable<T> c)  → unambiguous
```

                     ▼                 ▼

The HLD insight: nothing about target typing exists at runtime — by the time the platform runs, each lambda has already been compiled into a concrete functional-interface instance. The architecture simply shows that one callback-shaped lambda can register against several different APIs (fill handler, pricer, retry predicate) because the compiler resolved its type from each call site.
sections.s5d_lld:
**What is LLD?** Zoom into the compile-time rules: how the compiler infers a lambda's type from context, and how overloaded methods can cause ambiguity that forces an explicit cast.

```
  ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
       LLD — Target Typing & Overload Ambiguity (FAANG Level)
  ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Strategy (SAM): lambda becomes whatever functional type fits     │
  │  Callback registration: APIs accept behavior as parameters        │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: each lambda target type carries one responsibility            │
  │  O: new callback API = new overload, call sites type-infer        │
  │  D: methods accept functional-interface types, not concretes      │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── How the compiler assigns a type (target typing) ───────
   The lambda () -> ... has NO type by itself. The compiler looks at:
     1. Assignment target:   Runnable r = () -> doIt();
     2. Method parameter:    submit(() -> doIt());   (param type wins)
     3. Cast:                (Callable<Integer>) () -> 42;
     4. Return position:     return () -> doIt();     (return type wins)
   From that CONTEXT it picks the matching functional interface.

  ── Overload Ambiguity (the trap) ─────────────────────────
   void handle(Consumer<Order> c)      // returns nothing
   void handle(Function<Order,String> f)// returns a value
     handle(o -> process(o));          // if process returns void → Consumer
     handle(o -> o.getId());           // AMBIGUOUS? both could match
     // FIX: cast → handle((Function<Order,String>) o -> o.getId());

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. orderService.onFill(f -> ledger.credit(f.account(), f.amount()))
  2.   compiler sees onFill(Consumer<Fill>) → lambda typed as Consumer<Fill>
  3. orderService.priceOf(o -> o.qty().multiply(o.price()))  BigDecimal
  4.   compiler sees priceOf(Function<Order,BigDecimal>) → Function
  5. Rajesh SAV2001 order filled → Consumer.accept(fill) runs at runtime
```

The LLD answers the question directly: a lambda is poly-expression with no standalone type. The compiler assigns its type from the target context — the variable it is assigned to, the method parameter it is passed to, the cast applied, or the return position. When two overloads both structurally accept the lambda, the call is ambiguous and the developer must disambiguate with an explicit cast to the intended functional interface.
sections.s6_takeaway:
A lambda expression has no intrinsic type. The compiler determines its functional interface type from the target context: the variable it is assigned to, the method parameter it is passed to, the return type of the enclosing method, or an explicit cast. The same lambda `() -> "RELIANCE"` can be a Supplier, a Callable, or any functional interface with a compatible signature, depending purely on where it appears.

In my trade execution engine, I demonstrate all four contexts: a variable typed as Supplier makes the lambda a Supplier, a variable typed as Callable makes the identical lambda a Callable, a method parameter type determines the lambda type, and a return type determines it. The ambiguity problem occurs when a method is overloaded with two different functional interfaces that have the same lambda-compatible signature. Both Supplier.get and Callable.call accept no arguments and return a value, so a lambda `() -> result` matches both. The compiler cannot choose and reports "reference to method is ambiguous."

The fix is either an explicit cast like `(Supplier<TradeResult>) () -> result` to tell the compiler which interface you mean, or assigning the lambda to a typed variable first and passing the variable. The best practice is to avoid overloading methods with different functional interface parameters that have the same lambda shape — use different method names instead: `processSync` for Supplier and `processAsync` for Callable. This eliminates the ambiguity entirely and makes the code self-documenting.

### 6.3 Functional interface (Q6 of 125) — FULL FORMAT

answers.question: What is a functional interface (SAM), what are examples from java.util.function, and is @FunctionalInterface mandatory?
answers.shortTitle: Functional interface — SAM, @FunctionalInterface, core interfaces

s1_definition.profdef: A functional interface has exactly ONE abstract method (SAM — Single Abstract Method). Can have any number of `default` and `static` methods. `@FunctionalInterface` is NOT mandatory but recommended — makes the compiler verify only one abstract method exists. Core interfaces: `Predicate<T>` (T → boolean), `Function<T,R>` (T → R), `Consumer<T>` (T → void), `Supplier<T>` (() → T), `BiFunction<T,U,R>` (T,U → R), `UnaryOperator<T>` (T → T), `BinaryOperator<T>` (T,T → T).
s1_definition.oneliner: A functional interface is any interface with exactly one abstract method (SAM), so it can be the target of a lambda — `default` and `static` methods don't count against it.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A functional interface has exactly ONE abstract method (SAM — Single Abstract Method). Can have any number of `default` and `static` methods. `@FunctionalInterface` is NOT mandatory but recommended — makes the compiler verify only one abstract method exists. Core interfaces: `Predicate<T>` (T → boolean), `Function<T,R>` (T → R), `Consumer<T>` (T → void), `Supplier<T>` (() → T), `BiFunction<T,U,R>` (T,U → R), `UnaryOperator<T>` (T → T), `BinaryOperator<T>` (T,T → T).

**One line to remember:** A functional interface is any interface with exactly one abstract method (SAM), so it can be the target of a lambda — `default` and `static` methods don't count against it.

sections.s2_technical:
A functional interface is an interface with exactly one abstract method — a Single Abstract Method (SAM) type. That single method is the target a lambda implements. The `@FunctionalInterface` annotation is optional but recommended: it makes the compiler fail if someone accidentally adds a second abstract method.

Java ships core functional interfaces in `java.util.function`: `Predicate<T>` (takes T, returns boolean) for rules like "is this trade large"; `Function<T,R>` (takes T, returns R) for transformations like `Trade -> BigDecimal`; `Consumer<T>` (takes T, returns nothing) for side effects like auditing; and `Supplier<T>` (takes nothing, returns T) for lazy factories like `() -> LocalDateTime.now()`.

A functional interface may ALSO declare `default` and `static` methods and still qualify, because those are not abstract. For example `Predicate` has a `default and(Predicate)` combinator so you can write `isLarge.and(isForeign)`. Senior nuance: methods of `Object` (like `equals`) do not count toward the single-abstract-method rule, which is why `Comparator` can declare `equals` and still be functional.
sections.s3_banking: Problem — National Bank of India wanted a pluggable "fraud rule" that teams could supply as a lambda, but a plain interface with two abstract methods silently broke lambda use. Fix: marking the rule interface `@FunctionalInterface` guarantees a single abstract method, so any team can plug in a lambda like `txn -> txn.amount() > LIMIT`.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Input: a transaction amount of Rs.20,00,000 checked against a fraud rule.

**Step 2.** `FraudRule` is a SAM interface; the lambda `amt -> amt > 1000000` implements its single `isSuspicious` method.

**Step 3.** `big.or(tiny)` uses the default combinator to produce a new `FraudRule` that is true if either rule fires — no new class written.

**Step 4.** `combined.isSuspicious(2000000)` calls `big` first, which returns true, so short-circuit makes the whole rule true.

**Step 5.** A Rs.5,000 amount triggers neither rule, so the combined rule returns false.

```text
INFO: amount 2000000 suspicious = true
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  @FunctionalInterface FraudRule { boolean isSuspicious(amount); }
    │  single abstract method = SAM → lambda target
    ▼
  big  = amt -> amt > 1,000,000
  tiny = amt -> amt < 1
    │  default or(...) combinator
    ▼
  combined = big.or(tiny)
    │ isSuspicious(2,000,000)
    ├─ big: 2,000,000 > 1,000,000 ? YES → true (short-circuit)
    └─ (tiny not evaluated)
    ▼
  result: true
```
sections.s5c_hld:
HLD is the rooftop view of the whole system. A functional interface is simply a type with exactly one abstract method (a SAM — Single Abstract Method), which means a lambda can stand in for it. Architecturally this is the foundation that lets behaviour be passed around like data: a Trade Processing Service can be wired with a Predicate for filtering, a Function for transforming, a Consumer for side effects, and a Supplier for factories — and swapping any of them is just passing a different lambda. The HLD shows that configurable processing pipeline inside the service layer.

For this topic, National Bank of India's trade processing pipeline is assembled entirely from functional interfaces composed together: isActive.and(isLarge) to filter, a Function to map to amounts, a Consumer to audit. Each SAM is a lambda, swappable at runtime.

```
  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
       HLD — Trade Processing (Functional Interface / SAM)  FAANG
  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  ┌─────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐
  │ Web Portal  │   │ FIX Gateway  │   ← Client Layer
  └──────┬──────┘   └──────┬───────┘
         │ HTTPS           │ FIX
         └────────┬────────┘
                  ▼
        ┌──────────────────────┐
        │     API Gateway      │  ← JWT, rate limit, routing
        └──────────┬───────────┘
                   │ REST POST /api/v1/trades/process
                   ▼
        ┌──────────────────────────────┐
        │  Trade Processing Svc (×4)   │  ← Application Layer
        │  SAM = 1 abstract method     │
        │  Predicate (filter)          │  lambda plugs into each
        │  Function  (map)             │
        │  Consumer  (audit)           │
        │  Supplier  (default)         │
        └───────┬──────────────┬───────┘
          Redis │              │ JDBC + Kafka
          GET   ▼              ▼
  ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐
  │ Redis Cluster│   │ PostgreSQL (Primary)  │   │ Kafka        │
  │ rule cache   │   │ - trades table        │   │ trade.audit  │
  │ TTL 5m       │   └──────────┬────────────┘   └──────────────┘
  └──────────────┘              │ WAL
                                ▼
                     ┌──────────────────────┐
                     │ Read Replica (×2)     │
                     └──────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Observability: Grafana, ELK (Consumer logs),     │
  │  Jaeger trace, PagerDuty alerts                   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Every stage of the pipeline is a functional interface filled by a lambda. Because each is a SAM, the compiler and runtime treat the lambda as that type, and the Trade Processing Service stays generic and reconfigurable.
sections.s5d_lld:
Zoom inside the Trade Processing Service. A functional interface has one abstract method; that is what makes a lambda assignable to it. @FunctionalInterface is the optional compile-time guard. The core family (Predicate.test, Function.apply, Consumer.accept, Supplier.get) covers the common signatures, and their default helpers (and, andThen) let you compose them like building blocks.

```
  ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
       LLD — Trade Processing (SAM functional interfaces)  FAANG
  ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────────┐

  │     WHY: pass filter/map/consume logic in; service code unchanged │
  │  Command Pattern: Consumer<Trade> = an action object to run       │
  │     WHY: encapsulate the audit side effect as a first-class value │
  │  Composition: Predicate.and / Function.andThen chain behaviours   │
  │     WHY: build the whole pipeline from small reusable SAMs        │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  │  S: each SAM does ONE thing (test / map / consume / supply)       │
  │  O: new behaviour? new lambda; pipeline wiring untouched          │
  │  L: any Predicate<Trade> substitutes wherever a Predicate is used │
  │  I: each interface is a single-method, focused contract           │
  │  D: service depends on the SAM interfaces, not concrete lambdas   │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐
  │ <<interface>>    │ │ <<interface>>    │ │ <<interface>>    │
  │ Predicate<T>     │ │ Function<T,R>    │ │ Consumer<T>      │
  │ + test(t):bool   │ │ + apply(t):R     │ │ + accept(t):void │  ← each SAM
  │ (SAM)            │ │ (SAM)            │ │ (SAM)            │
  └────────┬─────────┘ └────────┬─────────┘ └────────┬─────────┘
           └────────────────────┴───────────┬────────┘
                                             │ used by
                                             ▼
                        ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
                        │        TradeProcessingService         │
                        │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
                        │  - keep: Predicate<Trade>             │ ◇ strategy
                        │  - toAmt: Function<Trade,BigDecimal>  │ ◇ strategy
                        │  - audit: Consumer<Trade>             │ ◇ command
                        │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
                        │  + process(trades): BigDecimal        │
                        └───────────────────────────────────────┘

  1. Controller.process(trades)
  2.   → TradeProcessingService.process(trades)
  3.     → Predicate keep = isActive.and(isLarge)   compose SAMs

  7.     → .reduce(ZERO, BigDecimal::add)              aggregate
  8.  → return BigDecimal total
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A functional interface has exactly one abstract method and represents a function type that lambdas can implement. The core interfaces cover all common function signatures: Predicate for filtering (returns boolean), Function for transformation (takes T returns R), Consumer for side effects (takes T returns nothing), Supplier for factories (takes nothing returns T). They are composable: `isActive.and(isLarge)` chains two Predicates. In my trade processing service, the entire pipeline is built from functional interfaces composed together.

### 6.3 (Q7 of 125)

answers.question: What is a functional interface (SAM interface), what are examples from java.util.function, how does @FunctionalInterface help, is it mandatory, can a FI extend another interface, and can it have default and static methods?
answers.shortTitle: Functional interface — SAM, @FunctionalInterface, core java.util.function interfaces

s1_definition.profdef: A functional interface has exactly ONE abstract method (SAM — Single Abstract Method). It can have ANY number of `default` methods (with body) and `static` methods — only the abstract method count matters. `@FunctionalInterface` is OPTIONAL but strongly recommended: it makes the compiler verify that exactly one abstract method exists — accidentally adding a second causes a compile error. A functional interface CAN extend another interface as long as the resulting interface still has exactly one abstract method. Core interfaces in `java.util.function`: `Predicate<T>` (T to boolean — filtering), `Function<T,R>` (T to R — transformation), `Consumer<T>` (T to void — side effects), `Supplier<T>` (nothing to T — factory/lazy creation), `BiFunction<T,U,R>`, `UnaryOperator<T>` (extends Function, same input/output type), `BinaryOperator<T>` (extends BiFunction, all same type — used in reduce).
s1_definition.analogy: A functional interface is like a bank form with exactly ONE blank to fill in: the Predicate form has "Is this trade valid? YES/NO." The Function form has "Convert this trade to a receipt." The Consumer form has "Process this trade (no response needed)." The Supplier form has "Generate a new trade ID." You can add instructions (default methods) and stamps (static methods) to the form — but there is only ONE blank for the customer to fill in. `@FunctionalInterface` is the quality control stamp that says "I verify this form has exactly one blank."

sections.s3_banking:
**Problem — The bank's trade validation system has 15 different validation rules scattered across the codebase as separate classes.** Each class implements a `TradeValidator` interface with a `validate` method. Adding a new rule requires creating a new class file. The team refactors to use functional interfaces: each rule becomes a lambda or method reference, rules compose with `.and()` and `.or()`, and common rules are shared as static factory methods.

**What the project will show:** Custom @FunctionalInterface with default composition methods (and, or, negate), static factory methods for common validators, all 7 core functional interfaces used in a trade processing pipeline, and a validation engine that composes rules dynamically.

**Step 1.** Request: validate TRD-003. EntityManager loads the trade from PostgreSQL.

**Step 2.** The composed validator is built: `hasAccountId().and(hasSymbol()).and(hasPositiveQuantity()).and(validSide()).and(maxAmount(10M))`. This is a CHAIN of 5 TradeValidator lambdas connected by `.and()` default methods.

```
  ═══ @FunctionalInterface ANATOMY ═══

  @FunctionalInterface
  interface TradeValidator {
      boolean validate(Trade trade);                    // 1 ABSTRACT — lambdas implement THIS

      default TradeValidator and(TradeValidator other);  // DEFAULT — does NOT count
      default TradeValidator or(TradeValidator other);   // DEFAULT — does NOT count
      default TradeValidator negate();                   // DEFAULT — does NOT count

      static TradeValidator hasAccountId();              // STATIC — does NOT count
      static TradeValidator hasSymbol();                 // STATIC — does NOT count
  }
  // Total abstract: 1. Total default: 3. Total static: 2. VALID functional interface ✅

  ═══ COMPOSITION ═══

  TradeValidator composed = hasAccountId()     // rule 1
      .and(hasSymbol())                         // rule 1 AND rule 2
      .and(hasPositiveQuantity())               // ... AND rule 3
      .and(validSide())                         // ... AND rule 4
      .and(maxAmount(10M));                     // ... AND rule 5

  composed.validate(trade):
    hasAccountId? → "" → FALSE → short-circuit → return FALSE
    (hasSymbol, hasPositiveQuantity, validSide, maxAmount NEVER CALLED — short-circuit!)

  ═══ 7 CORE FUNCTIONAL INTERFACES IN PIPELINE ═══

  Predicate<Trade>:         trade -> trade.isActive()          → stream.filter()
  Function<Trade,BigDecimal>: Trade::getAmount                 → stream.map()
  Consumer<Trade>:          trade -> log.info(trade.id())      → stream.forEach()
  Supplier<String>:         () -> UUID.randomUUID().toString() → Optional.orElseGet()
  UnaryOperator<BigDecimal>: amount -> amount * taxRate        → List.replaceAll()
  BinaryOperator<BigDecimal>: BigDecimal::add                  → stream.reduce()
  BiFunction<Trade,BigDecimal,Trade>: (trade, fee) -> withFee  → Map.compute()
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A functional interface has exactly one abstract method. The FunctionalInterface annotation is optional but recommended as a compile-time guard that prevents accidentally adding a second abstract method. Default methods and static methods do not count toward the abstract method limit — they have implementations. This means a functional interface like Predicate can have one abstract method (test) plus three default methods (and, or, negate) plus one static method (not) and still be a valid functional interface that lambdas can implement.

In my trade validation engine, I created a custom TradeValidator functional interface with one abstract method (validate), three default composition methods (and, or, negate), and five static factory methods (hasAccountId, hasSymbol, hasPositiveQuantity, validSide, maxAmount). Each factory returns a lambda implementing the validate method. The composition methods return new lambdas that chain the original validators. This replaces 15 separate validator classes with 15 one-line lambdas that compose fluently: `hasAccountId().and(hasSymbol()).and(maxAmount(10M))`. Adding a new validation rule means adding one static factory method — no new class file, no modification to existing code.

The seven core functional interfaces in java.util.function cover all common function signatures: Predicate for boolean results used in filtering, Function for transformation used in mapping, Consumer for side effects used in forEach, Supplier for lazy value creation used in orElseGet, UnaryOperator for same-type transformation used in replaceAll, BinaryOperator for same-type reduction used in reduce, and BiFunction for two-argument functions used in Map.compute. These compose with methods like andThen, compose, and, or, and negate — enabling complex behavior from simple building blocks without creating intermediate classes.

answers.question: Is @FunctionalInterface mandatory? Can a functional interface extend another? Can it have default and static methods?
answers.shortTitle: @FunctionalInterface on non-functional, extend non-functional, default+static methods

s1_definition.profdef: `@FunctionalInterface` is optional but recommended: it makes the compiler verify exactly one abstract method exists — adding a second accidentally causes a compile error. A functional interface CAN extend another non-functional interface (as long as the result has exactly one abstract method). It CAN have any number of `default` and `static` methods — only the abstract method count matters. Lambdas still work because they implement the single abstract method.
s1_definition.oneliner: `@FunctionalInterface` is optional documentation that makes the compiler enforce the single-abstract-method rule — the interface works with lambdas with or without it.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `@FunctionalInterface` is optional but recommended: it makes the compiler verify exactly one abstract method exists — adding a second accidentally causes a compile error. A functional interface CAN extend another non-functional interface (as long as the result has exactly one abstract method). It CAN have any number of `default` and `static` methods — only the abstract method count matters. Lambdas still work because they implement the single abstract method.

**One line to remember:** `@FunctionalInterface` is optional documentation that makes the compiler enforce the single-abstract-method rule — the interface works with lambdas with or without it.

sections.s2_technical:
The `@FunctionalInterface` annotation is NOT mandatory for an interface to be functional — any interface with exactly one abstract method can be a lambda target. The annotation is a compile-time safety net: it makes the compiler reject the interface if it ever has zero or more than one abstract method.

A functional interface CAN extend another interface, but only if the combination still yields exactly one abstract method. If a sub-interface re-declares the same method signature as its parent, it is still one abstract method, so it stays functional. If it adds a second, different abstract method, it is no longer functional and `@FunctionalInterface` fails to compile.

A functional interface can freely add `default` and `static` methods — these have bodies, so they are not abstract and do not break the single-abstract-method count. Methods inherited from `Object` (such as `toString`, `equals`) also do not count. A banking example: a `SettlementStep` interface extends a base `Named` interface that only has default methods, so `SettlementStep` still has one abstract `apply` method and remains a valid lambda target. Senior nuance: adding the annotation documents intent and prevents a future teammate from accidentally breaking every lambda call site.
sections.s3_banking: Problem — A teammate added a second abstract method to the bank's `SettlementStep` interface, which silently broke dozens of lambda call sites across the settlement service. Fix: the `@FunctionalInterface` annotation turns that mistake into a compile error, so the single-abstract-method contract is enforced before code ships.

sections.s6_takeaway:
FunctionalInterface annotation is optional but strongly recommended as a compile-time guard. A functional interface can have unlimited default and static methods — only the single abstract method matters for lambda compatibility. Default methods enable composability: `validator1.and(validator2)` chains validators. Static factory methods like `TradeValidator.minAmount(1000)` create common validators without a class. This pattern is used throughout java.util.function: Predicate.and, Predicate.or, Function.andThen.

**Step 1.** Request: calculate fees for TRD-001 (RELIANCE, 100 × Rs.2450.50 = Rs.245,050).

**Step 2.** `FeeCalculator.percentageFee(0.001)` creates a lambda: `trade -> trade.getAmount().multiply(0.001)`. This is the ONE abstract method implemented.

**Step 3.** `.withMinimum(20)` calls the DEFAULT method which returns a NEW lambda that wraps the original: `trade -> { fee = original.calculate(trade); return fee < 20 ? 20 : fee; }`. The original lambda is captured in a closure.

**Step 4.** `.withMaximum(2500)` wraps AGAIN: another layer that caps at Rs.2500. Three lambdas chained.

**Step 5.** `composed.calculate(trade)` executes the chain: inner lambda calculates 0.1% = Rs.245.05, middle lambda checks minimum (245 > 20 — OK), outer lambda checks maximum (245 < 2500 — OK). Final: Rs.245.05.

**Step 6.** For small trade TRD-002 (Rs.4,208): 0.1% = Rs.4.21. Minimum check: 4.21 < 20 → returned Rs.20.

**What is LLD?** Zoom into the FraudRule interface to show that @FunctionalInterface is optional, a functional interface MAY have default and static methods and MAY extend another interface (as long as it still has exactly one abstract method).

```

       LLD — Custom Functional Interface Rules (FAANG Level)
  ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Strategy (SAM): FraudRule is a one-method strategy = a lambda    │
  │  Composite via default and()/or(): combine rules into one rule    │
  │  Static Factory: FraudRule.always()/never() prebuilt rules        │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: each rule tests ONE condition                                 │
  │  O: new rule = new lambda, engine code unchanged                  │
  │  I: FraudRule has a single abstract method (true SAM interface)   │
  │  D: engine depends on FraudRule abstraction, not concrete rules   │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   <<@FunctionalInterface>> FraudRule        │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────────────│
  │  + check(txn: Txn): Risk        1 ABSTRACT  │  ← the SAM
  │  + default and(other): FraudRule            │  allowed (compose)
  │  + default or(other): FraudRule             │  allowed
  │  + static always(): FraudRule               │  allowed (factory)
  │  + static never(): FraudRule                │  allowed
  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘
     (can also: interface FraudRule extends BaseRule, if BaseRule
      adds no extra abstract method — still exactly one SAM)

  ── Facts the diagram encodes ──────────────────────────────
   • @FunctionalInterface is OPTIONAL (doc + compile guard only).
   • Default and static methods DO NOT count toward the SAM count.
   • A functional interface MAY extend another interface if the
     total abstract-method count stays at exactly one.
   • Object methods (equals/hashCode/toString) are NOT counted.

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. FraudRule highValue = txn -> txn.amount().compareTo(LIMIT)>0 ? HIGH : LOW;
  2. FraudRule foreign   = txn -> txn.isForeign() ? HIGH : LOW;
  3. FraudRule combined  = highValue.and(foreign);   default method
  4. engine.evaluate(txn Rajesh SAV2001 Rs.900,000)
  5.   → combined.check(txn)                          SAM invoked
  6.   → Risk.HIGH → publish fraud.alert to Kafka
```

The LLD answers the question precisely: `@FunctionalInterface` is not mandatory — any interface with a single abstract method is already functional and usable as a lambda target. The annotation only makes the compiler enforce the single-abstract-method rule. A functional interface can freely add default and static methods (they do not count toward SAM) and can extend another interface as long as the combined abstract-method count remains exactly one.
sections.s6_takeaway:
The FunctionalInterface annotation is not mandatory — any interface with exactly one abstract method is a functional interface and can be used with lambdas. However, the annotation is strongly recommended because it provides compile-time safety: if someone accidentally adds a second abstract method, the compiler immediately reports an error at the interface definition instead of at every lambda usage site across the codebase. This is the same principle as Override — technically optional but prevents subtle bugs.

In my brokerage fee service, the FeeCalculator functional interface has one abstract method (calculate), three default composition methods (withMinimum, withMaximum, withDiscount), and three static factory methods (flatFee, percentageFee, tieredFee). Each factory returns a lambda. Each default method wraps the current lambda in a new lambda that adds a rule. This creates a composable pipeline: `FeeCalculator.percentageFee(0.001).withMinimum(20).withMaximum(2500)` produces a fee calculator that computes 0.1% of the trade amount, ensures at least Rs.20, and caps at Rs.2500 — all from composing one-line lambdas without any class hierarchy.

A functional interface can extend another interface as long as the combined result still has exactly one abstract method. If the parent has an abstract method, the child must override it as a default method to keep the SAM count at one. This pattern is used by UnaryOperator extending Function and BinaryOperator extending BiFunction in the standard library. Default and static methods do not count toward the abstract method limit because they have implementations — the lambda only needs to implement the single abstract method.
