answers.question: What is Stream.mapMulti (Java 16) — it pushes 0..N elements to a Consumer instead of returning a sub-stream like flatMap — when is it more efficient, and how do you use it?
answers.shortTitle: Stream.mapMulti (Java 16) — push 0..N elements imperatively, vs flatMap

s1_definition.profdef: `mapMulti(BiConsumer<T, Consumer<R>>)` (Java 16) is an intermediate operation where you PUSH elements to a downstream Consumer instead of creating a Stream (like flatMap). For each input element, you call `consumer.accept(output)` zero, one, or many times. More efficient than flatMap when: (1) producing 0 or 1 elements per input (no Stream.of/Stream.empty overhead), (2) imperative logic is needed (loops, conditions), (3) avoiding per-element Stream object allocation.
s1_definition.analogy: flatMap: each clerk creates a TRAY of items and puts the tray on the belt. mapMulti: each clerk directly PLACES items on the belt one by one — no tray needed. For one or zero items per clerk, skipping the tray saves time.
s1_definition.oneliner: mapMulti((element, consumer) → { consumer.accept(output); }) = push elements imperatively. Fewer intermediate Stream objects than flatMap. Java 16+.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `mapMulti(BiConsumer<T, Consumer<R>>)` (Java 16) is an intermediate operation where you PUSH elements to a downstream Consumer instead of creating a Stream (like flatMap). For each input element, you call `consumer.accept(output)` zero, one, or many times. More efficient than flatMap when: (1) producing 0 or 1 elements per input (no Stream.of/Stream.empty overhead), (2) imperative logic is needed (loops, conditions), (3) avoiding per-element Stream object allocation.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** flatMap: each clerk creates a TRAY of items and puts the tray on the belt. mapMulti: each clerk directly PLACES items on the belt one by one — no tray needed. For one or zero items per clerk, skipping the tray saves time.

**One line to remember:** mapMulti((element, consumer) → { consumer.accept(output); }) = push elements imperatively. Fewer intermediate Stream objects than flatMap. Java 16+.

sections.s2_technical:
`Stream.mapMulti` (Java 16) is an imperative alternative to `flatMap` for one-to-many mapping. Instead of returning a new stream per element, you receive a `Consumer` ("downstream") and PUSH zero or more output elements into it: `stream.mapMulti((trade, downstream) -> { if (trade.isSplit()) { downstream.accept(leg1); downstream.accept(leg2); } else downstream.accept(trade); })`.

The advantage over `flatMap` is efficiency when each element usually produces zero or one result, or a small known number: `flatMap` allocates a `Stream` object per element even to emit one value, whereas `mapMulti` just calls `downstream.accept` with no intermediate stream allocation. This matters in hot paths over large datasets.

A banking example: expanding block trades into their constituent legs — most trades emit themselves (one accept), but a block trade emits several legs — done with `mapMulti` to avoid creating a throwaway stream for the common single-leg case. Senior nuance: prefer `flatMap` for readability when each element naturally maps to a collection/stream; reach for `mapMulti` as a performance optimisation when the per-element stream allocation of `flatMap` is measurable, or when the emission logic is naturally imperative.
sections.s3_banking: Problem — Expanding block trades into legs with `flatMap` allocated a throwaway stream for every trade, even the common case of a single-leg trade, hurting a hot settlement path. Fix: `mapMulti` pushes output legs into a downstream consumer with no per-element stream allocation, so single-leg trades cost nothing extra and block trades emit multiple legs.

### 6.47 toArray overloads (Q123 of 125) — FULL FORMAT

answers.question: How do the toArray() overloads work — toArray() returns Object[], while toArray(IntFunction<A[]>) / toArray(String[]::new) returns a typed array — and why do you need the generator?
answers.shortTitle: Stream.toArray() vs toArray(IntFunction) — Object[] vs typed array

s1_definition.profdef: `stream.toArray()` returns `Object[]` — the element type is erased due to generics. `stream.toArray(String[]::new)` returns `String[]` — the generator function `IntFunction<A[]>` creates an array of the correct type. The generator receives the array size and returns a new typed array: `size -> new String[size]`. This is equivalent to `toArray(String[]::new)` using constructor reference. Without the generator, Java cannot create a typed array because `new T[]` is illegal due to type erasure.
s1_definition.oneliner: toArray() → Object[]. toArray(String[]::new) → String[]. Generator needed because `new T[]` is illegal (type erasure). Constructor reference `Type[]::new` is the idiomatic generator.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `stream.toArray()` returns `Object[]` — the element type is erased due to generics. `stream.toArray(String[]::new)` returns `String[]` — the generator function `IntFunction<A[]>` creates an array of the correct type. The generator receives the array size and returns a new typed array: `size -> new String[size]`. This is equivalent to `toArray(String[]::new)` using constructor reference. Without the generator, Java cannot create a typed array because `new T[]` is illegal due to type erasure.

**One line to remember:** toArray() → Object[]. toArray(String[]::new) → String[]. Generator needed because `new T[]` is illegal (type erasure). Constructor reference `Type[]::new` is the idiomatic generator.

sections.s2_technical:
`Stream.toArray()` with no arguments returns an `Object[]` — you lose the element type, so you cannot treat it as `String[]` without casting each element. `Stream.toArray(IntFunction)` takes an array constructor reference and returns a TYPED array: `stream.toArray(String[]::new)` returns a `String[]`.

The typed form is almost always what you want because it preserves compile-time type safety and avoids `ClassCastException` at use sites. The `IntFunction` you pass (`String[]::new`) receives the required length and allocates an array of the correct component type, into which the stream elements are copied.

A banking example: converting a stream of account IDs to a `String[]` for a legacy API that requires an array — `ids.stream().toArray(String[]::new)` — rather than `(String[]) ids.stream().toArray()` which fails because the runtime array is actually `Object[]`. Senior nuance: never cast the no-arg `toArray()` result to a typed array; it throws `ClassCastException` because the array's runtime component type is `Object`. Always use `toArray(Type[]::new)` for typed arrays.
sections.s3_banking: Problem — Converting a stream of account IDs to a `String[]` for a legacy API used `(String[]) stream.toArray()`, which threw `ClassCastException` because the array was really an `Object[]`. Fix: `stream.toArray(String[]::new)` passes an array constructor so the result is a genuine, type-safe `String[]`.

### 6.47 (Q124 of 125) — FULL FORMAT

answers.question: What are stream characteristics / Spliterator flags (ORDERED, SIZED, SORTED, DISTINCT, NONNULL, IMMUTABLE, CONCURRENT), and how do they let the pipeline optimize?
answers.shortTitle: Spliterator characteristics/flags — ORDERED, SIZED, SORTED, DISTINCT and pipeline optimization

s1_definition.profdef: Spliterator characteristics are bit flags that describe properties of the stream source. The stream pipeline uses them to OPTIMIZE execution: `SIZED` enables pre-allocated result containers (ArrayList of exact size). `ORDERED` ensures encounter order is preserved — absence allows forEach to run unordered in parallel. `SORTED` lets sorted() become a no-op if the source is already sorted. `DISTINCT` lets distinct() become a no-op if elements are already unique. `NONNULL` means no null elements. `IMMUTABLE` means the source won't be modified during traversal. `CONCURRENT` means the source supports concurrent modification safely.
s1_definition.analogy: The conveyor belt has LABELS: "SORTED by amount" (SORTED), "exactly 100 items" (SIZED), "all unique" (DISTINCT). If the belt is labeled SORTED and you ask to sort it — skip! Already done. If labeled SIZED, the packing machine pre-cuts a box of exactly 100 slots. These labels let the factory SKIP unnecessary work.
s1_definition.oneliner: SIZED = pre-allocate. ORDERED = preserve order. SORTED = skip sort. DISTINCT = skip distinct. Flags enable the pipeline to skip redundant operations.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Spliterator characteristics are bit flags that describe properties of the stream source. The stream pipeline uses them to OPTIMIZE execution: `SIZED` enables pre-allocated result containers (ArrayList of exact size). `ORDERED` ensures encounter order is preserved — absence allows forEach to run unordered in parallel. `SORTED` lets sorted() become a no-op if the source is already sorted. `DISTINCT` lets distinct() become a no-op if elements are already unique. `NONNULL` means no null elements. `IMMUTABLE` means the source won't be modified during traversal. `CONCURRENT` means the source supports concurrent modification safely.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The conveyor belt has LABELS: "SORTED by amount" (SORTED), "exactly 100 items" (SIZED), "all unique" (DISTINCT). If the belt is labeled SORTED and you ask to sort it — skip! Already done. If labeled SIZED, the packing machine pre-cuts a box of exactly 100 slots. These labels let the factory SKIP unnecessary work.

**One line to remember:** SIZED = pre-allocate. ORDERED = preserve order. SORTED = skip sort. DISTINCT = skip distinct. Flags enable the pipeline to skip redundant operations.

sections.s2_technical:
A `Spliterator` is the engine under every stream: it both describes how to traverse elements (`tryAdvance`) and how to split them for parallelism (`trySplit`). Its CHARACTERISTICS are bit flags that let the stream pipeline optimise. Key flags: `ORDERED` (elements have a meaningful encounter order), `SIZED` (the exact count is known up front), `SORTED` (already sorted by some comparator), `DISTINCT` (no duplicates), `NONNULL`, and `IMMUTABLE`/`CONCURRENT`.

These flags drive optimisations. If a source is `SIZED`, the pipeline can pre-allocate the result array and even skip a `peek` whose output is unused for `count()`. If it is already `SORTED` with the right comparator, `sorted()` becomes a no-op. If it is `DISTINCT`, a later `distinct()` can be skipped. An `ArrayList` spliterator is `ORDERED` and `SIZED` and splits cheaply (great for parallel); a `HashSet` is `DISTINCT` but not `ORDERED`; a `LinkedList` splits poorly.

A banking example: streaming an `ArrayList` of trades in parallel is efficient because its spliterator is `SIZED` and splits in O(1), while the same over a `LinkedList` is slow. Senior nuance: choose the source collection for the stream workload — array-backed sources give `SIZED`/`ORDERED` spliterators that parallelise and optimise well; understanding characteristics explains why `sorted()`/`distinct()` sometimes cost nothing and why parallel speedups depend on the source.
sections.s3_banking: Problem — A parallel trade aggregation was slow because it streamed a `LinkedList`, whose spliterator splits poorly and is not SIZED, defeating parallelism. Fix: back the data with an `ArrayList`, whose spliterator reports SIZED/ORDERED and splits in O(1), so the parallel pipeline can pre-size results and balance work across cores.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Spliterator characteristics are optimization hints that the stream pipeline reads before execution. SIZED means the element count is known — the pipeline pre-allocates result containers of exact size. SORTED means elements are already sorted — sorted() becomes a no-op. DISTINCT means elements are unique — distinct() becomes a no-op. ORDERED means encounter order matters — the pipeline must preserve it. Absence of ORDERED allows parallel forEach to skip coordination. These flags are why `treeSet.stream().sorted()` is instant (source is already SORTED) while `arrayList.stream().sorted()` buffers all elements.

answers.question: What are Java Records (Java 16), what do they auto-generate, and when should you use them vs regular classes?
answers.shortTitle: Records — immutable data carriers, auto-generated methods, when to use

s1_definition.profdef: A `record` is a compact, immutable data carrier class introduced in Java 16. `record Trade(String id, BigDecimal amount) {}` auto-generates: (1) private final fields for each component, (2) canonical constructor, (3) accessor methods (id(), amount() — NOT getId/getAmount), (4) equals() based on all components, (5) hashCode() based on all components, (6) toString() showing all components. Records are final (cannot be extended), cannot have instance fields beyond the components, and components are immutable (final). Use records for DTOs, value objects, tuples, and any class whose identity is defined by its data.
s1_definition.analogy: A record is like a bank receipt: it has fixed fields (date, amount, account), is SEALED (you can't add extra notes after printing), and two receipts with the same data are considered EQUAL. You don't write getDate()/equals()/hashCode()/toString() for every receipt — the receipt PRINTER (compiler) does it automatically.
s1_definition.oneliner: `record Trade(String id, BigDecimal amount) {}` = immutable, auto equals/hashCode/toString, accessor methods id()/amount(). Use for DTOs and value objects. Java 16+.

Records are final (cannot be extended), cannot have instance fields beyond the components, and components are immutable (final). Use records for DTOs, value objects, tuples, and any class whose identity is defined by its data.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A record is like a bank receipt: it has fixed fields (date, amount, account), is SEALED (you can't add extra notes after printing), and two receipts with the same data are considered EQUAL. You don't write getDate()/equals()/hashCode()/toString() for every receipt — the receipt PRINTER (compiler) does it automatically.

sections.s2_technical:
A record is an immutable data carrier declared in one line: `record Trade(String id, BigDecimal amount) {}`. The compiler generates a canonical constructor, a private final field and public accessor for each component, and value-based `equals`, `hashCode`, and `toString`. Records are implicitly final and cannot extend a class (they can implement interfaces).

You can add a COMPACT canonical constructor to validate or normalise: `record Trade(String id, BigDecimal amount) { Trade { if (amount.signum() < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException(); } }`. Because records are immutable and value-based, two records with equal components are equal, which makes them ideal as map keys, DTOs, and events. Record patterns (Java 21) deconstruct them in `switch`/`instanceof`.

A banking example: modelling a `TransferRequest(String from, String to, BigDecimal amount)` as a record gives a concise, immutable DTO with correct equality for free, safe to share across threads and to use as a cache key. Senior nuance: use records for data-centric, immutable aggregates (DTOs, events, value objects); do NOT use them where you need mutability, inheritance, or encapsulated behaviour-rich domain entities — those remain classes.
sections.s3_banking: Problem — Transfer DTOs were verbose classes with hand-written constructors, getters, equals, hashCode, and toString that drifted out of sync and caused subtle equality bugs as cache keys. Fix: a `record TransferRequest(String from, String to, BigDecimal amount)` auto-generates a correct immutable carrier with value-based equality, safe to use as a map key and across threads.

Records (Java 16) are immutable data carriers that auto-generate constructor, accessor methods (id() not getId()), equals, hashCode, and toString from the component declaration. `record Trade(String id, BigDecimal amount) {}` replaces 50+ lines of POJO boilerplate. Records are final, cannot extend classes, cannot have mutable fields, and component accessors use component names (not JavaBean naming). Use records for DTOs, value objects, map keys, and any class whose identity is its data. The compact constructor `Trade { validate(); }` enables validation without repeating parameter assignments. Records + sealed classes + pattern matching = modern Java's algebraic data types.
